content: Bachelor of Science (BSc) degrees are awarded to students who focus primarily on scientific, medical, or technical disciplines. Bachelor of Arts (BA) degrees, on the other hand, are conferred upon students who concentrate on humanistic, theological, or jurisprudence fields. Since the late 1990s, bachelor’s degrees have also been introduced in professional areas such as nursing and teaching. These professional bachelor’s degrees typically require four years of study at a college. However, unlike traditional bachelor’s degrees awarded by universities, these professional degrees do not automatically grant access to a university master’s program. In France, the traditional bachelor’s degree is equivalent to the French Licence, which is a three-year degree. Following the implementation of the European LMD Bologna process in 2004, the French higher education system now includes a three-year bachelor’s degree, a two-year master’s degree, and a doctoral program that requires three or more years of study. In Germany, bachelor’s degrees, historically referred to as Bakkalaureus, existed but were abolished in 1820 as part of educational reforms. The Magister degree, originally a graduate-level qualification, became the first degree after five years of study. In 1899, the Diplom degree was introduced as a second first-degree option when technical universities (Technische Hochschulen) gained university status. However, in 1998, new educational legislation reintroduced the bachelor’s degree as the first degree after three years of study. These degrees are now referred to as either Bakkalaureus or Bachelor, with the English term being more commonly used. The traditional degrees were phased out by 2010. In Italy, the Bologna Process replaced the old five-year Laurea system. The current BA-level degree is called Laurea, which was briefly renamed Laurea Triennale after the reforms. This degree typically takes three years to complete and allows access to postgraduate degrees, such as the Laurea Magistrale (equivalent to a master’s degree), which was also briefly renamed Laurea Specialistica. To graduate, students must complete 180 credits and submit a thesis. Graduation marks range from 66 to 110, with some universities awarding a maximum of 100. A distinction, or lode, may be granted to students achieving a perfect score of 110/110 in recognition of an excellent thesis. Graduates with BA/BSc or MA/MSc degrees in Italy are addressed as Dottore (for men) or Dottoressa (for women). In the Netherlands, the degree system was restructured in 2004 to align with international standards. Former degrees such as baccalaureus (bc., equivalent to MA or MSc) and ingenieur (ing., for graduates of universities of applied sciences) are still awarded alongside their international equivalents. Bachelor’s degrees are granted by both accredited colleges and universities. However, bachelor’s degrees from universities allow direct entry into master’s programs, while those from colleges often require an additional bridge year (or pre-master year) to qualify for master’s programs. This distinction arises because university bachelor’s programs include research training, whereas college programs do not. In Poland, the licencjat degree is equivalent to the bachelor’s degree in Anglophone countries. In Russia and Ukraine, the Specialist degree was historically the first academic qualification in the Soviet Union. In the early 1990s, the Bakalavr (bachelor’s) degree was introduced across the Commonwealth of Independent States, except in Turkmenistan. After earning a Bakalavr degree, students can pursue a master’s degree, which requires an additional one to two years of study. The old five-year Specialist degree system is being phased out in universities participating in the Bologna Process, and new students no longer have this option. In Switzerland, similar to Austria and Germany, there was no tradition of bachelor’s degrees. The traditional first degrees were the Licentiate and the Diplom, while the second degrees were the DEA and the Postgraduate Diploma. Bachelor’s and master’s degrees replaced these older qualifications in 2003. In countries following the British tradition, such as the United Kingdom, medical students pursue undergraduate medical education and are awarded bachelor’s degrees in medicine and surgery (e.g., MB BChir, BM BCh, MB ChB, or MB BS). Historically, at Oxford and Cambridge universities, students first earned a BA degree after three years of medical study, followed by the BM BCh or MB BChir degree upon completing the clinical stage of their training.
